ecosystem.e: From eco- + system. Coined by English botanist Arthur Tansley in 1935 in a paper titled The Use and Abuse of Vegetational Concepts in the journal Ecology.

d.g: Terrorism with an ecological motive, such as attacks against corporations perceived to be harming the natural environment.

ectasia.e: From Ancient Greek ἐκτασία (ektasía), from ἔκτασις (éktasis, “a stretching out”) + -ία (-ía, abstract noun suffix), from ἐκτείνω (ekteínō, “to stretch out”) + -σῐς (-sĭs), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) + τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”).

The lengthening of a syllable from short to long.

ectasis.e: Ancient Greek ἔκτασις (éktasis)bor. English ectasis Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἔκτασις (éktasis).

d.g: Theoretical body type in which a person has a high metabolism. Such a person can easily maintain a low fat physique, but does not add muscle or body weight easily.

ectomorph.e: Derived from ectoderm + -morph from William Herbert Sheldon. Equivalent to ecto- + -morph.

A parasite that lives on the surface of a host organism; such as the Demodex mite, which lives in human hair and eyelashes.

ectoparasite.e: From ecto- (from Ancient Greek ἐκτός (ektós, “outside”)) + parasite.

d.g: The condition where an organ or other body part has an abnormal position.

ectopia.e: Learned borrowing from New Latin ectopia, derived from Ancient Greek ἔκτοπος (éktopos, “away from a place”), from ἐκ- (ek-) + τόπος (tópos). By surface analysis, ec- + -topia.
